prompt: TASKYou are a researcher deciding final inclusion for a systematic review screening. Studies that are included through this decision on the title-abstract level will go on to full text screening for a final inclusion decision. You will be provided with a title and abstract from a scientific research paper. Your task is to decide whether this research paper fulfills the below specified inclusion rules. This is the iteration 2.5GOALMake a binary decision to either include or exclude the research paper based on the input in the form of the title and the abstract of a study. The goal with this title-abstract screening is 100% precision with the highest recall possible. Your decision should be Boolean (`true` or `false`). Return the answer `true`, if the title and abstract comply with the inclusion rules specified below.INCLUSION RULESTwo types of inclusion criteria need to be met, to include the research paper.Formal inclusion rules:Title and abstract are displayed Language of the title and abstract is EnglishPublication type is sourced from academic literatureSubstantive inclusion rules:The research paper needs to evaluate a government policy or a trial.The government policy or trial evaluated needs to mitigate climate change.The study design of the research paper needs to use experimental, quasi-experimental or inferential research methods or conduct a systematic review.Keep in mind that we are optimising for precision on the title and abstract level but eventually will analyse the full-text. Even if not all criteria are explicitly met in the abstract, you can reasonably determine if the inclusion criteria will be met in the full-text. We are rather inclusive at the abstract-screening level.Each rule is further specified in the following paragraphs.FORMAL INCLUSION CRITERIATo include a record it needs to meet the following formal criteria:Title and abstract are displayed Some titles and abstracts may be missing in the database, due to access restrictions by publishers. If the title or abstract is missing, incorrectly displayed, or shortened, such that there is insufficient information to make an inclusion/exclusion decision, exclude the study.Language of the title and abstract is EnglishAt this stage of the project we cannot capture non-English titles and abstracts. Exclude studies that are not in English.Publication type is sourced from academic literatureThe records screened at this stage should generally all be eligible for the evidence bank. As we are currently only screening records from a single literature repository, we expect only peer-reviewed literature and academic preprints. Both should be included. Bachelor, master or PhD theses, non-academic types of publications, conference abstracts, should be excluded.SUBSTANTIVE INCLUSION CRITERIA If all three criteria are met, then the record should be included. If any of the questions are answered negatively, then the record should be excluded. The three headline questions are the following, with further clarifying details set out further below:Is a government policy or trial mentioned and evaluated?Is the policy intended to deliver climate mitigation?Is the study design eligible?Note: the outcome variable of the policy evaluation is of no importance here. The inclusion criteria focuses on the policy’s aim and the study design. Any outcome evaluated is of interest to us, including those related to the implementation, public acceptability or political feasibility of the measure.Note: At this first stage of inclusion screening based on title and abstract, we consider it more important to be overly inclusive (with the risk of including irrelevant records) than to be overly exclusive (with the risk of excluding relevant records). Therefore in case of uncertainty with one of the three headline questions, we recommend including at this stage.Is a government policy or trial mentioned and evaluated?To include a record it has to mention the evaluation of at least one government policy or intervention. This either needs to be a policy already implemented by some level of government organisation or an intervention already trialed in an experiment, designed to inform future policy. Only include studies that use ex-post data, i.e policies that have already been implemented. Even if the abstract mentions a broad policy category, or several different policies, include. If a specific policy is not mentioned, as long as it is in a policy field relevant to us, we include.Government policies are eligible for inclusion if they cover any laws, fiscal and monetary instruments, information campaigns, public services, diplomatic actions or provision of infrastructure provided by local, national, or supra-national bodies of government. Studies whose main aim is to analyse public expenditure or government budgets are excluded as these are not policies per se.Trial interventions are eligible for inclusion where policy is implemented under experimental or quasi-experimental conditions. To qualify, the intervention must emulate a government policy instrument, meaning it must alter the incentive structure, rule structure, or information structure facing an actor (individual, household, firm, or institution) with the aim of inducing a change in behaviour. Trials that instead evaluate the technical performance, or practical feasibility of a technology or practice directly, such as technology readiness trials, are not eligible. Interventions by non-governmental organisations, implemented outside of a trial setting, are not eligible.Table 1: Examples of types of interventions considered government policies or trialsIncluded:National or Policies aiming for digitalisation (of public administration for example) with no explicit goal to increase electrification should not be included.Increase the use of low-carbon technologies: Policies fostering the use of low-carbon technologies and materials, such as nuclear power, carbon capture and storage, or low-carbon concrete. Foster modal shift in the transport sector: Policies incentivising or regulating a shift to lower carbon modes of transport, i.e. from cars, motorbikes or planes, to buses, trains, or active modes of transport (e.g. pricing of public transport, expansion of services in public transport, taxes or regulations on private vehicle use, expansion of cycling/walking lanes, etc.). Policies aiming for “sustainable transport” are assumed to have the aforementioned goals and are included.Foster a change towards more plant-based diets: Policies regulating or incentivising the demand or supply of food products in favour of plant-based products instead of meat products (e.g. tax incentives for plant-based diets, information campaigns, policies restricting meat production, etc.)The aim of a policy should not be determined too narrowly. We still consider policies relevant even if the aims specified above are not amongst those explicitly identified publicly by the government implementing the policy (or other actors implementing a relevant trial) as the main aim or motivation for the policy. For example, a fuel tax may be mainly motivated by its ability to raise government revenues. Still, the application of a fuel tax raises the fuel’s overall cost to consumers and is commonly associated with a reduction in the use of that fuel. It should therefore be included because an expected outcome is a reduction in fossil fuel use or reduction in energy consumption, which are both relevant outcomes set out in the list above.We also include studies, where the government policy or trial described in the title and abstract may not have a clear and apparent intention to deliver climate mitigation, but where the abstract mentions that it is evaluated for one of the above specified climate mitigation outcomes, e.g. it evaluates the impact on GHG emissions or energy consumption (for example, using PM 2.5, PM10, ozone or CO2 as outcome variables).The policy aims specified above are all defined in a manner that they strengthen climate mitigation. However, we also include the reversal or weakening of a relevant, implemented policy. For example, we should also include an evaluation of an energy efficiency standard that is removed, or weakened, the roll-back of renewable energy support policies, the lowering of a carbon tax.Policies labelled as “green”, “sustainable”, or “environmental”, with unclear mechanisms and intentions, that do not clearly align with the outcomes list above, should be excluded. ! study design eligible?The third criterion for inclusion is the study design, or method. We focus on including studies that provide ex-post evaluation of government-implemented policies and trials. In particular, we aim to include three types of study designs: quantitative ex-post evaluations of implemented policies, experimental study designs, and evidence syntheses thereof. However, these study designs are only INDICATIVE: if the authors state that they are evaluating a relevant policy (using the verb “evaluate”) at some point in their study, we include even if their methods seem descriptive or qualitative.Quantitative ex-post policy evaluations include all study designs using real world data and quantitative research methods to attribute the effect of the policy on the observed data. This includes:quasi-experimental research designs: difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity designs, synthetic control methods, instrumental variable designs other inferential research methods: panel regression designs, time-series methods, cross-sectoral studies, statistical analysis, etc. Experimental study designs particularly include randomised controlled trials, before/after experiments, treatment/control designs, lab-in-the-field and survey experiments (questionnaires).Evidence syntheses are included if the synthesised evidence covers study designs eligible according to the criteria above. Evidence syntheses include systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, meta-ethnographies, mixed-method syntheses, evidence and gap maps and systematic maps. Traditional literature reviews without any formal review methods and purely bibliometric assessments of the literature are excluded. We also exclude the following types of studies: purely qualitative research designs; purely descriptive assessments of data (descriptions of time trends, presentations of datasets, descriptive surveys, etc.); ex-ante modelling studies’ theoretical studies’ as well as comments, perspectives, or similar.!!!
